A 28–31 GHz dual-polarization transceiver board, from block diagram to fabrication-ready layout

I designed the complete PCB platform around two AKRONIC ALTUS28TR transceivers and a shared NEXUS28Z synthesizer, including its six-rail power network, and checked each high-risk block in LTspice or full-wave EM before fabrication.

In brief

The hard part of this project was keeping every block consistent with the same system assumptions, from the block diagram to the routed board: component choices, interface circuits, supply rails, controlled-impedance routing and digital control.

What I designed

  • The system architecture: two polarization branches, a shared LO plan, baseband interfaces and the TDD control scheme.
  • The power network: six rails from a 5 V input, using three buck modules, an inverting buck converter and two LDOs.
  • Baseband conditioning with LTC6409 and ADA4927 fully differential amplifiers.
  • GCPW routing on a hybrid RO4350B stackup and the full six-layer layout in KiCad.
  • A Python host framework for TDD timing and RF-switch control.

How I verified it

  • LTspice for the four switching rails: startup, load steps, ripple before and after filtering, and output impedance.
  • LTspice for both baseband interfaces, in time and frequency domain, with non-ideal component models.
  • Full-wave EM in RFPro for the two riskiest structures, extracted from the real layout geometry.
  • Simulated TDD frame sequencing and waveform spectra from the Python framework.

What is not done yet

  • The board was not fabricated within the thesis timeline, so no result on this page is a measurement.
  • The two LDO rails were not simulated in detail, so their behavior rests on datasheet PSRR and noise data.
  • EM verification covers two local structures, not the full board.

Figure numbers on this page match the thesis PDF, so every plot can be traced to the full text.

Architecture

Two ALTUS28TR transceivers handle one polarization each. A single NEXUS28Z PLL feeds both local-oscillator inputs, so the two branches share one frequency reference. Two Red Pitaya STEMlab 125-14 boards generate and capture the analog I/Q signals, and a USB-to-SPI bridge configures every IC from the host PC.

The ALTUS28TR is a zero-IF transceiver: it translates I/Q baseband straight to RF through the local oscillator, with no intermediate frequency. LO quality and distribution therefore become board-level design problems. The shared reference lets the polarizations operate coherently, but their final relative phase still depends on LO routing, path lengths and board tolerances, which is why the LO fan-out on the board is symmetric.

The NEXUS28Z covers 7.9–9.8 GHz. With the ×3 LO multiplication inside the ALTUS28TR, the on-board source reaches about 23.7–29.4 GHz at RF, so operation above roughly 29.4 GHz uses the external LO input that the board provides through its own connector.

Power delivery

The board needs six supply rails with very different noise budgets. The mmWave transceivers and the PLL are sensitive to ripple, the amplifier stages need a bipolar supply, and the digital side only needs a clean 3.3 V. The whole network runs from a single 5 V input.

At the power entry, an SMAJ5.0A TVS diode clamps surges and hot-plug transients, and a 22 µF bulk capacitor with a 100 nF bypass keeps the input impedance low for every downstream regulator.

Switching where the current is, linear where the noise is

A linear regulator dropping 5 V to 2.6 V at 750 mA would dissipate P = (VIN − VOUT) IOUT ≈ 1.8 W on that rail alone. The three heavier positive rails therefore use TPSM82822 buck modules, which integrate the inductor in the package. The −2.5 V rail uses a TPS63710 synchronous inverting buck with an external inductor. The 1.8 V PLL rail and the 3.3 V digital rail carry little current, so an LDO costs little efficiency there, and the PLL gets an ultra-low-noise TPS7A2118-Q1 kept isolated from the switching rails, because supply noise on a PLL shows up directly as LO phase noise.

Setting each output

Each converter output is set by a resistive feedback divider, VOUT = VREF(1 + RTOP/RBOT). The inverting converter regulates against a negative reference.

Where the rails sit on the ripple curve

For a buck converter the first-order inductor ripple is ΔIL ≈ VIN D(1 − D) / (L fSW), a parabola in duty cycle that peaks at D = 0.5. From a 5 V input the three buck rails sit at D ≈ 0.36, 0.50 and 0.52, all within 8% of that worst case. Duty cycle offers no room to reduce ripple here. Inductance and switching frequency do, which is why a high-frequency module with an integrated inductor suits these rails. Pick a rail, or drag the output voltage, and watch the ripple follow the curve.

Idealized waveforms with the same L and fSW for every setting. They show the shape and the relative ripple, not the TPSM82822’s absolute values.

Filtering at the point of load

Each switching output passes through a ferrite bead and a second local decoupling network before it reaches the IC pins. The bead raises the impedance seen by high-frequency conducted noise, and the local capacitors shunt that noise to ground close to the load. Placement is hierarchical: small capacitors sit at the pins for fast transient current, larger ones near the regulator for low-frequency storage. The bead sits after the regulated node, outside the converter’s feedback loop, so its DC resistance appears as a small load-dependent drop at the load.

In the layout, the regulators share one PDN region and each rail runs locally to its load instead of through a shared supply structure, which limits common-impedance coupling between domains. Switching nodes stay away from feedback nodes and low-noise branches. Every rail also has an external injection pad and a jumper, so it can be powered and checked on its own during bring-up.

Verification in LTspice

I simulated each switching rail with its regulator model, output capacitance, bead stage, local decoupling and a pulsed load. The 2.6 V rail, the heaviest positive branch, ran under a 0.7 A load.

Steady-state results per switching rail (thesis section 4.7).
RailConverterRipple before beadRipple at the loadDC drop across bead
1.8 V coreTPSM82822≈ 6 mVppsub-mV≈ 7 mV
+2.5 V FDATPSM82822≈ 10 mVppsub-mV≈ 9 mV
2.6 V RF, 0.7 ATPSM82822≈ 10 mVppsub-mV≈ 20 mV
−2.5 V FDATPS63710≈ 2 mVppsub-mV≈ 12 mV

The last column shows the trade-off. The bead removes the switching ripple, but on the 2.6 V rail it costs about 20 mV of DC at 0.7 A, roughly 0.8% of nominal. The output impedance of that rail stays in the tens of milliohms at low frequency and falls to a few milliohms in the MHz region.

What these simulations do not show. The beads are modelled as simple R-L-C equivalents rather than vendor broadband models, so bead resonances and DC-bias saturation are not captured. The two LDO rails were not simulated. None of these numbers are measurements: the first job after fabrication is rail-by-rail bring-up through the injection pads.

Baseband interface

The Red Pitaya boards expose single-ended ±1 V ports into 50 Ω. The ALTUS28TR expects differential I/Q at a defined common-mode level. Fully differential amplifiers bridge the two, one stage per direction and per branch.

On the transmit side, an LTC6409 presents about 50 Ω to the Red Pitaya DAC, converts the single-ended signal to a differential pair and sets the ALTUS28TR input common mode near 0.5 V through a buffered reference. On the receive side, an ADA4927 provides gain, DC-level translation and differential-to-single-ended conversion, driving the ADC with a ground-centered signal.

I simulated the TX path with its full external network, including the common-mode bias, split termination, series damping, non-ideal resistor models and the PCB launch, and extracted the impedances seen from both sides.

QuantitySimulated result
TX input impedance seen by the Red Pitaya DAC≈ 50 Ω across the usable band

RX drive into the Red Pitaya ADC≈ 2 Vpp, ground-centered

Layout and stackup

At 30 GHz a trace is a transmission line and every pad, via and connector launch is a discontinuity. The board itself becomes part of the RF circuit.

RF and LO lines use grounded coplanar waveguide: the coplanar ground with via fencing contains the field and holds the impedance better than plain microstrip in a dense layout. The top-layer geometry, 0.30 mm wide with 0.10 mm gaps, targets 50 Ω against In1.Cu, the ground plane 170 µm below it.

The stackup is a cost decision as much as an electrical one. RO4350B (Dk 3.48, loss tangent about 0.0037 at 10 GHz) fills only the two outer dielectric regions where the mmWave lines run, and standard S1000-2M laminate fills the inner core for power planes and control routing. The construction is mirrored around the 0.70 mm core so that the different thermal expansion of the two materials does not warp the board after reflow.

Each polarization branch reaches its 2.92 mm connector through a MASW-011145 SPDT switch that performs the TDD changeover. The LO chain can select the on-board PLL or an external source, amplifies it, and splits it symmetrically toward the two transceivers, keeping only one vertical layer transition in the LO path.

Digital control runs through an FT232H USB-to-SPI bridge, with TXB0108 level translators serving the SPI targets at their native logic levels: 2.6 V for the transceivers and 1.8 V for the PLL. The whole design is captured as hierarchical KiCad schematics with one sub-sheet per domain, and it passes electrical and design-rule checks.

EM verification

Closed-form line estimates stop being reliable where pads, bends, vias and neighboring ports crowd together. I exported the two riskiest regions from the KiCad layout and solved them full-wave in RFPro.

I rebuilt the stackup layer by layer in the EM environment, placed ground-signal-ground ports at the physical launch points, refined the mesh around the signal paths and vias, and evaluated the exported S-parameters in an N-port circuit testbench.

LO transition

The first structure is the final LO fan-out from the splitter toward the two transceivers, about 2 mm long, including the one vertical transition kept in the LO path. Across the 8–11 GHz LO band the return loss stays above 30 dB and the insertion loss below 0.1 dB.

RF and TDD switch region

The second structure is the dense multi-port area around the MASW-011145 SPDT switch, where the connector transition, the local ground shape and the adjacent branches interact within a few square millimeters. It is the hardest test in the thesis, and it shows.

Representative in-band values across 28–31 GHz (thesis table 8).

A straight GCPW line of the same length would lose only 0.32–0.56 dB at 30 GHz. The extra loss comes from the curved routing, the pad transitions, the via environment and the compact multi-port geometry around the switch footprint. I flagged this region as the first item to revise in a second board revision.

Control and TDD

In time-division duplex, transmit and receive share one channel in alternating slots. Guard intervals give the RF switches time to change state, and those intervals define the GPIO sequence the host has to drive.

Default frame, 11 ms. TX 5.0 ms, guard 0.5 ms, RX 5.0 ms, guard 0.5 ms. The animation runs 400 times slower than real time, and the switch on the right follows the frame.

G
Antenna on the TX pathAntenna on the RX path

A modular Python framework on the host configures both Red Pitaya boards, defines the time slots and guard intervals, steps through the four frame states and drives the GPIO lines that switch the RF front-end. It also generates representative waveform classes for testing, whose spectra I checked in simulation.

Scope. Host-side Python timing jitters on the order of milliseconds, which stretches the frame. The framework is a bring-up and functional-test tool, not a deterministic timing controller. Tight TDD timing belongs in FPGA logic or another hardware-timed controller.

Limits and next steps

The thesis delivers a routed, DRC-clean, simulation-verified design package. It stops before fabrication, and it says so.

Limits of this work

  • No fabricated board, so no measured RF performance, timing margins or over-the-air results.
  • EM verification is local to the LO transition and the switch region. Connector launches, soldering, package tolerances, material variation and manufacturing spread sit outside the simulations.
  • Ferrite beads use simplified R-L-C models, and the baseband simulations use simplified models beyond the PCB boundary rather than the exact ALTUS28TR input and output behavior.
  • The on-board LO covers the band up to about 29.4 GHz, and above that the external LO input is required.

Next steps, in order

  1. Bring-up before any RF test: supply rails, jumper-selected domains, current draw, rail indicators and SPI communication.
  2. Measure the LO route from 8 to 11 GHz and the switch region from 28 to 31 GHz, and compare both against the EM extractions.
  3. Measure the shared LO path for amplitude and phase balance before any dual-polarization test.
  4. Test the Red Pitaya interface with the host software, then move TDD timing to hardware.
  5. Revise the geometry around the SPDT switch in a second board revision.
